source.question: e-5922
source.value:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/60ff5bf60ca0505446961f9bfae83d1ece21d53cd180fdd6a687dba1ca767b68.png)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 8 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3-(-3))^{2}+(5-5)^{2}+(-1-1)^{2}+(3-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/9cdf7153834225217e3cfd680182777f47f2cc0d09185a66742b46fc67ebd7b6.png)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & 9 \\ 9 & 27\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/4e59afb848b5180340b05874c2dd63d04c22186c0c8e2235535e19551cab983a.png)

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}2\right)= \dfrac\pi 4,
$$

which is already an acute angle, as desired.

source.value:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2,$ and $x_3$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $x_1 = 2x_2-3x_3.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/8aac548229fb8312eefaed282dd27daadf560b17009f163d568ca1edda949a69.png)

Consequently, 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/b241f88f83f96ef2f393b7450e5933831b300b98522b16b02208298db1b4ea91.png)
is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we let $A$ be a matrix whose columns equal the elements of $\mathcal B,$ and we find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
